column4: Its near-verbatim مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ states the section's knot directly: acquired wealth cannot suffice when ruin arrives.
The condemned person says مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ in his own voice, turning the section's claim that wealth will not suffice into a confession after judgment.
أَن رَّآهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ names exactly the self-perception of sufficiency carried by the miser in 92:8.
This ayah gives the consequence completed by 96:7: the human being transgresses when he sees himself as self-sufficient.
عُسْرَةٍ and مَيْسَرَةٍ stage the section's two roots as a debtor's financial constriction and restored means, while forgiving the debt reverses the miser's withholding.
The wealthy person must spend from his abundance, the constrained from what God gave him, and the ayah closes with God's promise to place ease after hardship.
The ayah joins miserliness and turning away, then corrects imagined self-sufficiency with وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ: God is rich and humans are needy.
Immediately after 111:2 says wealth did not avail Abu Lahab, this ayah supplies the consequence: entry into a flaming fire.
يَوْمَ لَا يَنفَعُ مَالٌ وَلَا بَنُونَ states the same boundary as 92:11 at the judgment scene: neither wealth nor children benefit.
Satan's promise of poverty gives the fear behind withheld wealth, while God's promise of forgiveness and bounty exposes that fear as a false measure of sufficiency.

At death's approach the holder of provision asks for a brief delay specifically so that he may give charity, staging the section's claim that wealth becomes useful only by being released before the fall.
وَوَجَدَكَ عَآئِلًا فَأَغْنَىٰ assigns enrichment to God and reverses the self-produced sufficiency imagined in ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ.
أَمَّا مَنِ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ identifies the self-sufficient-seeming man in the very encounter developed by the section.
This ayah supplies the response to 80:5: the Prophet directs his attention to the man who presents himself as self-sufficient.
لَا يَجْزِي وَالِدٌ عَن وَلَدِهِ gives the section's dictionary example of jazāʾ as being enough for another, then denies that sufficiency in both parent-child directions on the promised day.
لَن تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُهُم makes wealth and children unable to avail against God and places their owners at the fire.
This repeated formula again denies that wealth or children can avail against God and names the fire as the abiding outcome.
Neither wealth nor children can avail their owners against God here; the ayah makes the same possessions that signify abundance powerless before the fire.
Those who are miserly with what God gave them mistake withholding for good, but the withheld gift becomes a collar around them on resurrection day.
After God gives them from His bounty, they بَخِلُوا۟ بِهِۦ and turn away, exactly joining acquired abundance, miserliness, and the section's turning-away stance.
This ayah condemns those who are miserly, command others to be miserly, and conceal the bounty God has given them, defining wealth as entrusted provision rather than self-sufficiency.
The preceding question to 47:38 says that if God pressed people for their wealth they would become miserly, exposing what their attachment to possession contains.
Those who are miserly and command miserliness are answered with God's independence, so withholding harms no need in God and reveals only the holder's mistake.
The ayah remarkably joins stinginess with the section's secondary death sense: أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ and the gaze of one يُغْشَىٰ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْمَوْتِ.
نَظَرَ ٱلْمَغْشِىِّ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْمَوْتِ is the Quranic death-swoon wording that realizes the section's dictionary extension from night covering to death covering a person.
وَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes both enrichment and the giving of holdings to God; أَقْنَىٰ also meets the source section's qinyah language for acquired property.
Religious authorities who consume wealth wrongfully and hoard gold and silver instead of spending it enact the section's definition of withholding possessions from their due use.
The hoard of 9:34 is heated in the fire and brands its owners, making retained wealth itself testify to its failure to protect them.
جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ depicts the one who gathers and stores away, the clearest nonlexical parallel to holding acquired goods back.
The blaze calls the person who turned away; with 70:18 it joins the turning-away figure of surah 92 to gathered, hoarded wealth.
ٱلَّذِى جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ depicts wealth gathered and repeatedly counted, the possessed store on which false sufficiency rests.
The accumulator thinks his wealth has made him immortal, stating the precise illusion that money can survive or prevent the moment in 92:11.
كَلَّا لَيُنۢبَذَنَّ فِى ٱلْحُطَمَةِ breaks the immortality calculation of 104:3 by showing the hoarder cast into the Crusher.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, giving narrative form to the self-sufficient stance.
He enters his garden wronging himself and says it will never perish, transferring imagined personal sufficiency to his possessions.
When his produce is destroyed, he wrings his hands over what he spent on it; abundance has become empty-handed loss in a single scene.
After the garden falls, no party can help him besides God and he cannot help himself, marking the exact limit of possessions and social strength.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, whereas enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; the ayah distinguishes what is held briefly from what remains.
Qarun attributes his fortune to knowledge he possesses, a narrative instance of treating acquired wealth as self-sufficiency.
God makes the earth swallow Qarun and his house; neither his faction nor he can save him, vividly staging the fall at which accumulated wealth cannot avail.
Those who had desired Qarun's place now recognize that God expands and restricts provision, correcting their reading of abundance after his fall.
The garden owners are tested through property they assume they can harvest on their own terms, opening a scene of possession and withheld giving.
They make their plan without reservation, showing the confidence in continued possession that the night's destruction will undo.
A visitation from the Lord passes over the garden while they sleep, making loss arrive beneath the cover of night.
By morning the abundant garden has become stripped and dark, a literal passage from means to deprivation.
Their whispered order that no poor person enter the garden that day states the intended withholding of the poor person's share.
They go out resolved and believing themselves able to exclude, joining miserliness to imagined control over the crop.
On seeing the ruined garden they first think they have lost the way, registering how completely possession has vanished.
They finally say that they have been deprived, reversing their plan to deprive the poor person in 68:24.
A human reads generous provision as proof that his Lord has honored him, exposing the mistaken equation between abundance and worth.
When provision is measured tightly, the same person calls it humiliation; together with 89:15 this names the false moral reading of fullness and emptiness.
The correction begins by saying they do not honor the orphan, shifting the measure of honor from received wealth to its treatment of the vulnerable.
Failure to urge feeding the poor shows the withholding concealed behind the complaints about constricted provision.
Consuming inheritance greedily depicts acquisition without regard for another's due share.
An excessive love of wealth names the attachment that makes possession feel like sufficiency and giving feel like loss.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor fully outspread; this bodily image sets a measured boundary between miserliness and ruinous expenditure.
God expands provision and measures it, grounding the spending measure in 17:29 in divine rather than self-made sufficiency.
Humans would withhold even the treasuries of divine mercy for fear that spending exhausts them, and the ayah names the human being as tightfisted.
The servants' spending is neither extravagant nor miserly but measured between them, giving the behavioral balance absent from the self-sufficient hoarder.
An increase sought through other people's wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakat given seeking God's face is multiplied; this directly tests what gain and repayment mean.
Spending is to seek God's face, and whatever good is spent is repaid in full; this matches the giver who seeks no human repayment in 92:19-20.
The givers say they feed only for God's face and want neither جَزَآءً nor thanks, an explicit counterpart to giving without a favor to be repaid.
وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving a favor in order to obtain more, sharply defining the non-transactional giving described in the section.
Charity is taken from their wealth to purify and increase them, matching the giver of 92:18 who gives his wealth seeking purification.
The Helpers prefer others even while in privation, and success belongs to those protected from their own stinginess; need here becomes the setting for generosity.
The command to spend for one's own good and the promise of success to those protected from inner stinginess reverse the miser's claim that retaining wealth serves him.
A recognized right for the asker and deprived person exists within their wealth, directly specifying what must not be withheld from its claimant.
The worshippers' wealth contains a known right, defining property as carrying an obligation rather than conferring independence.
This ayah names the asker and the deprived person as the recipients of the known right in 70:24.
Attaining righteousness requires spending from what one loves, making release of valued possession rather than its retention the road to the good.
When commanded to spend from God's provision, the rejecters refuse to feed those in need and use providence itself as their excuse for withholding.
Withholding even ordinary aid is the small-scale form of keeping possessions from those to whom access should not be denied.
The good loan is multiplied by God, who also constricts and expands; giving, not hoarding, is placed within the true movement between scarcity and abundance.
God expands or restricts provision and replaces whatever is spent, answering the fear that released wealth leaves only lack.
If provision were expanded without measure, people would transgress; God sends it in due measure, joining abundance to the danger named in 96:6-7.
People come to God alone and leave behind everything He had conferred on them, making the death-bound loss of acquired possessions explicit.
A rejecter confidently claims that he will be given wealth and children, voicing the presumption that possession continues beyond accountability.
God inherits what the man claims in 19:77, and the man comes alone; the promised possessions pass away from their claimant.
The question asks whether the wealth and sons supplied to people are being mistaken for a hastening of good things.
The answer denies the inference in 23:55: abundant provision is not itself proof of good or favor.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and more children mean they will not be punished, stating the false immunity that 92:11 denies.
Wealth and children do not bring a person near to God; faith and right action supply the different measure and multiplied reward.
Noah's people follow one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss, reversing abundance into spiritual deficit.
Worldly rivalry in wealth and children is compared to growth that pleases and then withers into debris, showing acquired abundance passing away.
What people possess runs out, while what is with God remains; this is the clearest boundary between the held purse and lasting sufficiency.
Competition for increase distracts people, naming accumulation itself as the activity that masks its insufficiency.
The distraction of accumulation lasts until people reach the graves, placing its limit at precisely the death threshold developed in the section.
The human being's intense love of wealth identifies the attachment behind counting, withholding, and imagined self-sufficiency.
The graves being overturned sets the judgment boundary immediately after 100:8's love of wealth.
The stupor of death arrives with the truth one tried to evade, a direct nonlexical realization of the section's gloss about death's covering faintness.
فَتَرْدَىٰ uses the same ruin root as 92:11: denial of the Hour and preference following desire end in perishing.
A saved speaker tells his former companion إِن كِدتَّ لَتُرْدِينِ, preserving the root's causative sense of bringing someone to ruin.
لَا تَجْزِى نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْـًٔا denies that one soul can be enough or compensate for another on the day of judgment.
The repeated judgment warning again denies that one soul can compensate for another, reinforcing the boundary to every human repayment.
No soul possesses anything for another on that day and all command belongs to God, expressing the same failed interpersonal sufficiency without relying on wealth.
Even an earthful of gold offered as ransom is not accepted from one who dies rejecting faith, setting an absolute limit on wealth as compensation.
All that is on earth, doubled, cannot ransom the rejecters from the day’s punishment, enlarging the failed purse to its conceivable maximum.
Those who reject their Lord would ransom themselves with everything on earth and as much again, but possession cannot discharge that reckoning.
Even all earthly wealth doubled would be offered to escape the evil of judgment, making the wished-for payment explicitly insufficient.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ closely echoes the promise of being eased toward ease and preserves its directed, divinely enabled sense outside surah 92.
فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا places ease with hardship and supplies the plain semantic axis that the section hears again as wealth and poverty.
The repeated promise that ease is with hardship reinforces the axis rather than treating hardship as the final condition.
God intends ease and does not intend hardship for people; the explicit opposition grounds the section's literal yusr/ʿusr axis.
After 26:88 strips wealth and children of benefit, this ayah names the sound heart as what can meet God safely.
They give food they themselves value to the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9 then discloses a motive free of repayment or thanks.
Following God's enrichment in 93:8, the addressee must not oppress the orphan; received abundance is converted into responsibility.
Following God's enrichment in 93:8, the beggar must not be repelled, reversing the closed hand of the self-sufficient person.
Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their due treats part of one's possession as another's right rather than a private store.
The command to give relatives, the poor, and travelers their due is explicitly for those seeking God's face, meeting both rightful release and pure motive.
Those seeking their Lord's face spend secretly and openly from His provision, a close positive counterpart to giving without repayment.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so expenditure leads to divine increase rather than the loss feared by miserliness.
Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, relocating adequate repayment from recipient to Lord.
Those who spend secretly and openly hope for a commerce that will never perish, a deliberate alternative to the perishing commerce of accumulated wealth.
God pays their rewards in full and adds from His bounty, completing the imperishable commerce of 35:29 with true sufficiency and recompense.
The question why people do not spend is answered by God's inheritance of heaven and earth, exposing every human holding as temporary custody.
Fear of poverty after excluding the idolaters is met with a promise that God can enrich from His bounty, moving security away from retained trade.
If prospective spouses are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty; poverty is a condition He can change, not a final measure of worth.
Humans are the poor in need of God, while God alone is the Rich and Praiseworthy; this directly relocates true sufficiency.
If spouses separate, God can enrich each from His abundance, presenting sufficiency as His provision rather than possession of the other.
The person has not attempted the steep path, introducing moral difficulty as the route the possessor avoids.
Freeing a slave defines the steep path of 90:11 through costly release rather than acquisition.
Feeding on a day of hunger makes material constriction the very occasion for generous action.
The orphaned relative is one concrete recipient of the difficult generosity named by the passage.
The destitute person in misery is the other recipient, placing the giver beside the person at the extreme of empty-handed need.
Immediately after the confession that wealth did not avail, the speaker says his authority has perished too, extending insufficiency from property to power.
The warning says the addressee is not accountable for whether the self-sufficient man purifies himself, qualifying the attention given him in 80:6.
The other man comes actively seeking, beginning the human contrast to the one who presents himself as self-sufficient.
The seeker fears God, the stance opposite to self-sufficiency that explains why his approach matters.
The Prophet's distraction from the fearful seeker completes the reversal for which attention to the self-sufficient man is corrected.
God will not delay a soul once its term comes, closing the extension requested for charitable giving in 63:10.
Believers must spend good acquired things rather than defective ones they would dislike receiving, and the ayah ends by naming God as Rich and Praiseworthy.
Charity ruined by reminders and injury is like soil washed from bare rock; outward expenditure proves unable to yield when its motive is false.
Those who spend seeking God's pleasure resemble a firmly rooted garden yielding doubly, the fruitful counter-scene to 2:264's stripped rock.
A town enjoying secure, abundant provision is made to taste hunger after ingratitude, staging a collective descent from ease to constriction.
Doors of plenty open after warning is forgotten, but seizure comes suddenly at the height of rejoicing, showing abundance unable to secure its possessors.
Adversity is replaced by prosperity until the people flourish, then sudden seizure breaks their confidence in continued ease.
The garden owner expects both no Hour and a better resort if returned to his Lord, showing how wealth feeds confidence beyond death.
The companion tells him to acknowledge God's will and power on entering the garden, correcting self-attribution while the property still stands.
The companion warns that God may give him something better and strike the boastful man's garden, making both increase and loss God's disposal.
The warning that the garden's water may sink beyond recovery supplies the concrete means by which apparent abundance can empty.
Qarun's treasure is so abundant that even its keys burden a company, establishing the scale of possession that still cannot prevent his fall.
Qarun is told to seek the hereafter with what God gave him and to do good, identifying the use that could have made wealth serve rather than deceive.
Those dazzled by worldly life wish for Qarun's fortune, showing the social appeal of reading visible abundance as success.
People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and right action, supplying the counter-measure to Qarun's display.
After acknowledging wrongdoing, the garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost garden with something better, relocating future means in God.
The passage identifies the garden's destruction as punishment and points to a greater hereafter punishment, preventing the material loss from being read as merely accidental.
After the passage exposes greed for wealth, hell is brought near and the human being finally remembers at judgment.
The person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, reversing the earlier habit of consuming and retaining into too-late recognition.
At death the person asks to be sent back, closely paralleling the request for postponement in 63:10.
He wants to do good in what he left behind, but a barrier prevents return; the unspent opportunity cannot be recovered after death.
The soul reaching the collarbones marks the bodily threshold at which the section says held wealth slips from the hand.
The cry for someone to cure the dying person exposes the limits of every available means at that threshold.
The dying person realizes that separation has arrived, giving awareness to the moment of irreversible loss.
The person is driven to the Lord, locating final ownership and destination beyond the possessions now left behind.
The soul reaching the throat presents the same death threshold at which material sufficiency ends.
Those present can only watch the dying person, unable to make their resources sufficient for him.
The challenge to return the soul, if humans are truly unaccountable, makes their inability at death the test of claimed independence.
Wealth and children are not to impress: God makes them a means of torment in this life and their owners' souls depart in rejection.
The warning repeats that wealth and children may become worldly torment and accompany no saving sufficiency at death.
Wealth and children are a trial while the great reward is with God, so abundance tests its holder rather than certifying success.
Wealth and children are a trial, while immense reward is with God; this distinguishes possessed means from the final measure.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
Preferring the nearer life states the choice that makes worldly holdings appear sufficient.
The hereafter is better and more enduring, supplying the lasting side of the contrast to 87:16.
The addressee must not strain toward others' worldly splendor; the Lord's provision is better and more enduring.
God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in a worldly life that is only a brief enjoyment beside the hereafter.
When hardship touches a person he calls on God, but after a blessing he claims it came through his own knowledge, reenacting the move from need to self-sufficiency.
Those before made the same claim, but what they had earned did not avail them, answering self-attribution with failed acquisition.
The passage closes by asking whether they know that God expands and restricts provision, naming the true source of both states.
After mercy following hardship, a person calls it his own and expects the best even if returned to God, a clear self-sufficient reading of restored abundance.
When blessed, the person turns away, but adversity makes him pray at length; the two states expose the instability of his claimed independence.
God apportions livelihoods and raises some over others in degree, while His mercy is better than what people accumulate.
The ayah imagines roofs and stairways of silver for rejecters, beginning a deliberate devaluation of visible wealth.
Gold and luxury are called only enjoyment of worldly life, whereas the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
God expands and restricts provision, directly correcting the affluent boast in 34:35 that quantity of wealth proves immunity.
The people of Saba receive two gardens and are told to eat their Lord's provision gratefully, establishing conspicuous abundance as a gift.
When they turn away, the flood replaces the fruitful gardens with bitter growth, a collective movement from plenty to deprivation.
Their loss is named as recompense for ingratitude, giving the abundance-to-hardship reversal its moral relation.
The people leave behind gardens and springs at destruction, showing that possessed abundance does not accompany its holders.
Comforts in which they delighted are included among what is abandoned.
God makes another people inherit those goods, completing the transfer that empties ownership at the former holders' fall.
يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ repeats the primary covering sense of 92:1, the physical image from which the section extends toward death's swoon.
The repeated phrase يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ supplies another direct occurrence of night covering day.
Righteousness includes giving wealth despite loving it to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, askers, and captives, making release of valued property the proof of faith.
The answer about what to spend is the surplus beyond need, directly bringing adequacy and excess into the measure of giving.
Believers must spend from their provision before a day on which trade, friendship, and intercession cannot supply what was withheld.
Spending in God's way is pictured as one seed yielding seven hundred grains, reversing the miser's arithmetic of loss and gain.
Those who spend without following the gift by reminders or injury receive their reward from their Lord, separating giving from a claim upon its recipient.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and God's being Rich closes a warning against transactional giving.
God erases usury and causes charities to grow, reversing the apparent financial increase of taking and decrease of giving.
The accusation that God's hand is chained is answered by His hands being outspread and His spending as He wills, opposing divine generosity to the closed-hand image of miserliness.
At harvest, people must give the crop's due right; this directly answers the garden owners who try to exclude the poor from acquired produce.
Wealth spent to block God's path becomes regret and ends in defeat, showing that even expenditure cannot avail when directed toward the wrong end.
They covenant that if God gives from His bounty they will give charity and become righteous, setting up the broken promise and miserliness exposed in 9:76.
The people resented only after God and His messenger enriched them from divine bounty, locating their material sufficiency in a gift they then deny.
God purchases believers' lives and wealth for the Garden, presenting surrendered possession as the exchange that endures.
Worldly abundance is likened to flourishing vegetation whose owners think it under their control just before it is cut down, a direct nonlexical scene of plenty becoming nothing.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their deeds in full within it, establishing a merely present and exhaustible return.
The seekers of worldly return in 11:15 have only fire in the hereafter and find their works void, exposing the final insufficiency of that payment.
Joseph's plan for seven years of abundant cultivation and stored grain gives a concrete scene of provision accumulated in anticipation of constriction.
Seven severe years consume what was stored during the abundant years, staging the movement from fullness to hardship almost literally.
A year of rain and pressing follows the famine, completing the scene with restored abundance after constriction.
Joseph's brothers arrive under hardship with poor merchandise and ask for full measure and charity, placing generosity precisely at the meeting of need and limited means.
The faithful must spend secretly and openly before a day with neither sale nor friendship, setting a deadline on wealth's useful release.
At the destroyed people's fall, what they had earned did not avail them, a concise parallel to possessions failing at ruin.
A powerless slave who owns nothing is contrasted with one given good provision who spends privately and publicly, joining possession, ability, and release in one parable.
People of means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; pardon replaces the impulse to close the purse after injury.
Owners are told to give contracted slaves from the wealth God gave them, defining property as divine provision containing another person's route to freedom.
Long enjoyment does not avail people when the threatened punishment comes, extending the section's question from money to every benefit enjoyed before the fall.
Solomon says gratitude benefits the grateful person, while his Lord is truly Rich and Generous, relocating sufficiency from the receiver of treasure to its giver.
Creatures that do not carry their own provision are still provided for by God, countering the fear that security depends upon hoarding a store.
The question reminds people that God expands provision and restricts it, another direct formulation of the purse's fullness and emptiness under His measure.
Destroyed peoples possessed greater strength and آثار, yet what they earned did not avail them when judgment arrived.
The person seeking the hereafter's harvest receives increase, while the seeker of the worldly harvest gets only some of it and no share in the hereafter.
Neither what the condemned earned nor their protectors avail them against the waiting fire, closely matching wealth's failure at ruin.
God asks no provision from people and does not ask them to feed Him, clarifying that human giving can never be repayment of a divine need.
God alone is the Provider and possessor of firm strength, completing 51:57's denial that He needs what humans hold.
People must spend from what God has made them successors over, explicitly describing wealth as temporary custody rather than independent possession.
A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward, answering the fear that generosity only empties the hand.
People are told neither to grieve over what escapes them nor exult in what arrives, preparing the diagnosis of proud miserliness in 57:24.
The distribution rule prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich, making the social release of possessions an explicit boundary on accumulation.
The saving commerce of 61:10 consists in faith and striving with wealth and life, showing the use through which wealth can serve beyond death.
People leave the sermon for trade or amusement, but what is with God is better and God is the best provider.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; those so distracted are named the losers before the death-regret scene of 63:10.
The ayah asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, exposing the dependence hidden by apparent self-sufficiency.
At judgment the criminal wishes to ransom himself with his own children, a direct family form of the compensation that cannot suffice.
He would offer everyone on earth if it could save him, expanding the failed ransom to the largest imaginable worldly possession.
The command to give God a good loan and send good ahead promises that it will be found with God better and greater in reward.
The condemned man is given extensive wealth, establishing the abundance that feeds his later demand for still more.
Despite extensive wealth and an eased life, he greedily desires an increase, showing that abundance has not made him inwardly sufficient.
The food of hell neither nourishes nor avails against hunger, giving the section's 'does not suffice' sense a concrete and terrible object.
The boast that one has consumed abundant wealth makes the amount spent a claim of status, immediately before the surah tests whether he took the steep path of liberating and feeding.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is a direct social form of retaining provision instead of directing it to need.
Spending wealth merely to be seen by people is set against the section's giver who seeks God's face and no human repayment.
The Lord is the truly Rich and merciful and can remove one people and appoint successors, joining divine sufficiency to the fragility of human possession.
The offer of a commerce that saves from painful punishment introduces the enduring exchange whose price in 61:11 includes wealth.
The people on the heights tell the arrogant that their gathered numbers or resources did not avail them, extending insufficiency beyond money to accumulated support.
Jacob takes prudent measures for his sons yet states that he cannot avail them at all against God, marking the boundary of even parental protection.
Those favored in provision refuse to pass it to people under their authority so that they might share equally, a social expression of treating provision as exclusively one's own.
The parable immediately before 18:46 makes worldly life vegetation that flourishes with rain and then becomes wind-scattered debris.
Moses asks not to be burdened with difficulty because of forgetfulness; this preserves the ʿusr root's ordinary sense outside the section's financial extension.
The righteous person is promised the finest reward and an easy command, another moral setting in which ease is divinely directed.
God inherits the earth and everyone upon it, supplying the ultimate ownership behind each person's abandonment of acquired goods.
God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, repeating the section's abundance-constriction relation.
The sudden blast leaves people unable to make a bequest or return to their families, fixing the instant at which control of property and household ends.
The keys of heaven and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; ownership and its changing measure meet in one formulation.
On the decisive day no protector or relation can avail another and none are helped, another interpersonal boundary on compensating for someone else.
The condemned are told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them there, leaving humiliation when that enjoyment ends.
Each person's own striving is recompensed with the fullest recompense, helping distinguish divine repayment from giving in order to settle a human favor.
Neither relatives nor children benefit people on resurrection day, extending the insufficiency of possessions to the closest human bonds.
The husbands of Noah's and Lot's wives cannot avail them against God, a concrete relational instance of one person being unable to suffice for another.
The wished-for ransom expands from children to spouse and brother, showing intimate relationships treated as payments that still cannot save.
Human anxiety under harm precedes the withholding response to received good in 70:21, joining fear of constriction to the closed hand.
God says He made the man's worldly circumstances smooth and ample, supplying the ease from which the man's unsatisfied desire for increase in 74:15 arises.
People will be questioned that day about their enjoyed abundance, making worldly comfort an accountable trust rather than self-validating wealth.
